## Limitation

Operating over long agentic trajectories introduces several considerations worth discussing. First, long-horizon agentic documentation task requires computational resources because both input context and generated outputs can grow large over the trajectory. To prevent context explosion and excessive runtime, we impose a maximum trajectory length, which can cause rare failures where the agent terminates before completing a sub-task. Second, because the agent depends on the model’s reasoning ability, it may occasionally enter a repeated loop without completing the sub-task. Although the overall impact is minimal, with only 0.08% of components terminating without meeting the verification threshold in our experiments, this limitation should still be considered (Failure analysis in Appendix ). Future work should explore more efficient trajectory control, adaptive stopping criteria, and stronger recovery mechanisms.
Third, beyond the agent’s runtime behavior, our evaluation itself has a scope limitation. We evaluate at the component level information sufficiency because DevEval’s human-curated unit tests exist only at the function level, enabling objective, execution-based verification via Pass@k; this is a deliberate choice for metric rigor. We acknowledge it does not directly measure the standalone utility of higher-level documents, but our results offer indirect evidence: regeneration performance increases monotonically as context widens (Figure 3), showing that higher-level documents carry architectural information that materially aids regeneration.

## AI Use Statement

We used generative AI tools in the following ways:
(i) code development, including implementation of the proposed method, baselines, and experiment scripts; (ii) translation and text editing, for improving clarity and consistency of the manuscript; and (iii) figure and table preparation, including generating plotting scripts and formatting tables.
All AI-generated code was reviewed and tested by the authors. All figures, tables, and reported numbers were checked against the raw experimental outputs, and all references were verified by the authors against their original sources.
The AI tools did not serve as authors. The authors take full responsibility for the entire content of this paper, including all text, claims, figures, tables, references, and artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

##### Verify: Self-evaluation and cross-document conflict verification.

Repository-level documentation often describes the same functionality from multiple perspectives across files, so without verification these descriptions easily drift apart and degrade overall consistency. Therefore, Verify assesses each draft \hat{d}_{i} along two axes. First, a self-evaluation scores factual consistency, completeness, and helpfulness according to the agent’s system prompt instructions (See Table 4 in Appendix A.2), and second, a cross-conflict verification scores inconsistencies between \hat{d}_{i} and its dependency-related documents, each on [0,1] .

For the cross-conflict verification, inspired by NLI-based inconsistency detection for text summarization [64, 65, 66], we decompose \hat{d}_{i} into atomic claims via an LLM and verify each claim with a local NLI model against a trusted reference set from RepoMemory. This reference set contains only the dependency-related records whose verification score exceeds a threshold, so a low-quality document never becomes a conflict-checking criterion and early errors cannot propagate. The resulting contradiction rate serves as the cross-conflict score.
 \hat{d}_{i} passes Verify only if the average of two verified scores exceeds a threshold. Otherwise, the detected conflicts are returned as a conflict report in the next turn’s observation, prompting the agent to issue an additional Read or to re-Write the draft. If \hat{d}_{i} still fails to pass after the agent has reached its predefined maximum number of revisions, we commit the highest-scoring draft to RepoMemory to preserve coverage. More details are provided in Appendix .

##### Finish: Memory commit and trajectory continuation.
